• Chapter 7: Food of Class 4 Science in the DAV Dayanand Anglo-Vedic curriculum systematically introduces the fundamental biological requirement of living organisms for sustenance, energy, and growth.
• Food serves as the primary biological fuel that powers all internal physiological processes, physical movements, and metabolic activities occurring within the human body.
• Every living organism, ranging from microscopic entities to complex multi-cellular plants and animals, requires an uninterrupted and balanced supply of food to survive.
• The study of food encompasses its origin, its constituent chemical components known as nutrients, and the specific functional roles these components play in maintaining life.
• Food is scientifically defined as any nutritious substance that people or animals eat or drink, or that plants absorb, in order to maintain life, growth, and tissue repair.
• Without a regular intake of food, the human body would rapidly deplete its energy reserves, leading to fatigue, cellular damage, organ failure, and eventually death.
• The DAV curriculum emphasizes that food is not merely a source of satiety or a way to appease hunger, but a sophisticated biochemical toolkit necessary for structural integrity.
• Different types of food contain varied proportions of essential biochemical substances called nutrients, which are categorized based on their specific physiological functions.
• The primary nutrients essential for human survival and optimal health are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals, each fulfilling unique metabolic duties.
• In addition to the five major nutrients, dietary water and roughage (fiber) play critical roles in digestion, waste elimination, and internal temperature regulation.
• Food acts as the raw material for building new cells, repairing worn-out tissues, healing wounds, and facilitating the continuous process of physical development during childhood.
• The DAV Class 4 Science syllabus encourages students to observe their daily dietary intake and recognize that no single food item contains all necessary nutrients in exact amounts.
• Understanding the concept of food diversity helps young learners appreciate the rich agricultural heritage of India and the varied culinary traditions of different regions.
• Food consumption habits directly influence physical fitness, cognitive development, emotional well-being, and the overall longevity and quality of human life.
• The study of food sets the foundational baseline for more advanced biological concepts such as the human digestive system, balanced nutrition, and ecological food webs.

• Carbohydrates are scientifically classified as the primary and most readily available source of energy for the human body, often referred to as energy-giving foods.
• When consumed, digestive enzymes break down complex carbohydrates into simple sugars, primarily glucose, which is then transported via the bloodstream to all body cells.
• Cells utilize glucose in cellular respiration to generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the universal energy currency that powers physical actions and internal organ functions.
• Children, athletes, and individuals engaged in rigorous physical labor require higher quantities of carbohydrates to sustain their daily energy expenditure and prevent early fatigue.
• Major dietary sources of carbohydrates include cereals like wheat, rice, maize, millet, and starchy root vegetables such as potatoes, sweet potatoes, and tapioca.
• Sugars, which provide a quick burst of energy, are found naturally in fruits (fructose), milk (lactose), and table sugar (sucrose), as well as in honey and jaggery.
• Excessive consumption of simple sugars without adequate physical activity can lead to the conversion of surplus glucose into body fat, resulting in unwanted weight gain.
• Complex carbohydrates, found in whole grains and legumes, release energy slowly and steadily over an extended period, maintaining stable blood sugar levels throughout the day.
• Dietary fiber, a type of carbohydrate that human digestive enzymes cannot break down, plays an indispensable mechanical role in moving waste smoothly through the digestive tract.
• Starch is the principal form in which plants store their excess chemical energy, and it forms a major bulk of the human diet across almost all global cultures.
• The DAV curriculum stresses that while carbohydrates are vital for energy, relying solely on carbohydrate-rich foods results in an incomplete and unbalanced diet.
• Whole grain foods are nutritionally superior to refined flour products because they retain the outer bran and germ layers, which are rich in fiber and micronutrients.
• The sweet taste of ripe fruits and the comforting texture of cooked rice or chapati are direct sensory indicators of the presence of carbohydrates in our meals.
• Maintaining an optimal balance of carbohydrate intake prevents metabolic disorders such as obesity and type 2 diabetes while ensuring peak daily physical performance.
• Teachers utilizing these DAV academic notes must emphasize that energy-giving foods are the engine oil of the human machine, keeping all systems active and responsive.

• Proteins are designated as body-building foods because they supply the essential chemical building blocks required for physical growth, tissue repair, and structural development.
• Chemically, proteins are complex macromolecules composed of long chains of smaller units called amino acids, which are linked together by peptide bonds.
• The human body requires various amino acids to synthesize new proteins for muscles, skin, hair, nails, internal organs, hormones, and specialized immune system antibodies.
• Growing children require a substantially higher proportion of protein in their diets compared to adults because their skeletal and muscular systems are expanding rapidly.
• Dietary protein sources are broadly classified into two main categories: animal-based proteins and plant-based proteins, each offering distinct nutritional profiles.
• Animal-based proteins, found in meat, fish, poultry, eggs, milk, curd, and cheese, are termed complete proteins because they contain all essential amino acids in adequate amounts.
• Plant-based proteins, found abundantly in pulses (dals), beans, lentils, chickpeas, soybeans, and nuts, are often deficient in one or more essential amino acids.
• Vegetarians can easily meet their daily protein requirements by consuming a varied combination of plant proteins, such as mixing lentils with rice or wheat chapati.
• Protein deficiency in children leads to severe growth retardation, muscle wasting, delayed motor development, weakened immunity, and clinical conditions like kwashiorkor.
• The process of physical healing after injuries, surgeries, or burns relies heavily on an increased supply of dietary proteins to regenerate damaged skin and muscle cells.
• Hair and nails are composed almost entirely of a tough, fibrous structural protein called keratin, highlighting the visible everyday impact of protein consumption.
• Enzymes, which are biological catalysts that accelerate chemical reactions within the human body, are themselves specialized functional proteins without which life cannot proceed.
• The DAV curriculum highlights pulses, commonly known as 'dals' in Indian households, as the cornerstone of plant-based protein intake in traditional vegetarian diets.
• Careful cooking of protein-rich foods is necessary to break down tough cell walls and anti-nutritional factors, making the amino acids easier for human digestion.
• Integrating adequate body-building foods into every meal ensures that the body maintains its structural integrity, repairs daily cellular wear and tear, and grows strong.

• Fats and oils are classified in the DAV science curriculum as concentrated energy-giving foods that yield more than double the amount of energy provided by an equal weight of carbohydrates.
• In addition to supplying high caloric energy, fats act as an essential thermal insulating layer beneath the skin, helping the human body maintain its internal core temperature.
• Dietary fats provide mechanical cushioning for vital internal organs, protecting them from physical shocks, sudden impacts, and external injuries during movement.
• Fats are vital for the absorption, transport, and storage of fat-soluble vitamins, specifically Vitamins A, D, E, and K, which cannot dissolve in water.
• The two primary sources of dietary fats are animal sources and plant sources, possessing distinct chemical structures and varying impacts on cardiovascular health.
• Animal fats include butter, ghee, cream, lard, and the visible fat present in red meat, poultry skin, and whole milk dairy products.
• Plant fats, generally referred to as vegetable oils, are extracted from seeds, nuts, and fruits, including mustard oil, groundnut oil, sunflower oil, olive oil, and coconut oil.
• Dietary fats are further categorized into saturated fats and unsaturated fats based on the chemical bonding of their constituent fatty acid carbon chains.
• Saturated fats, predominantly found in animal products and tropical oils like palm and coconut oil, tend to be solid at room temperature and should be consumed in moderation.
• Unsaturated fats, found in liquid vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish, are considered healthier options that support heart health and help regulate cholesterol levels.
• Trans fats, artificially created through the industrial hydrogenation of liquid oils, are highly detrimental to health and are commonly found in processed and fried snack foods.
• Excessive accumulation of body fat due to overconsumption of calorie-dense fatty foods leads to obesity, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular complications later in life.
• The DAV textbook notes that while fats have a negative reputation due to over-consumption, a controlled amount of fat is absolutely indispensable for nerve function and cell structure.
• Brain tissue has a remarkably high fat content, utilizing specialized fatty acids to build the insulating myelin sheaths that facilitate rapid electrical signal transmission.
• Balancing fat intake by choosing healthy plant-based oils over heavy animal fats ensures sustained energy reserves without compromising long-term circulatory health.

• Vitamins and minerals are designated as protective foods because their primary biological role is to safeguard the human body against various diseases and infections.
• Although required in relatively small quantities compared to carbohydrates and proteins, vitamins and minerals are critical micronutrients that regulate complex metabolic pathways.
• Vitamins are organic compounds classified into two distinct groups based on their solubility: water-soluble vitamins (Vitamin C and the B-complex group) and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
• Vitamin A, abundant in carrots, papaya, green leafy vegetables, milk, and eggs, is essential for maintaining good eyesight, healthy skin, and robust mucosal tissue linings.
• Vitamin B-complex group (B1, B2, B6, B12) supports proper nerve function, red blood cell formation, energy metabolism, and the maintenance of a healthy digestive tract.
• Vitamin C, found in citrus fruits like oranges, lemons, amla (Indian gooseberry), and tomatoes, strengthens the immune system and is vital for healthy gums and wound healing.
• Vitamin D, often called the sunshine nutrient because human skin synthesizes it upon exposure to ultraviolet sunlight, is crucial for strong bones and teeth calcium absorption.
• Vitamin E acts as a powerful cellular antioxidant that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage, while Vitamin K is indispensable for normal blood clotting.
• Minerals are inorganic elements derived from the soil and water that plants absorb and animals ingest, forming an integral part of human bones, teeth, and body fluids.
• Calcium, found in milk, cheese, and green vegetables, works alongside phosphorus to build dense, rigid skeletal structures and maintain strong dental enamel.
• Iron is a vital mineral component of hemoglobin, the red protein responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to every living cell throughout the body.
• Iron deficiency leads to a common blood disorder called anemia, characterized by persistent fatigue, weakness, pale skin, and reduced cognitive concentration in children.
• Iodine, found in iodized salt and seafood, is essential for the proper functioning of the thyroid gland, which regulates overall body growth and metabolic rate.
• Potassium and sodium act as key electrolyte minerals that maintain fluid balance, nerve impulse transmission, and proper muscle contraction, including heart rhythms.
• The DAV curriculum teaches that colorful fruits and vegetables are the best visual indicator of a rich supply of protective micronutrients, promoting the 'eat a rainbow' habit.

• Water is the most abundant and vital component of the human body, constituting approximately 60 to 70 percent of total adult body weight and even higher in children.
• Although water does not provide direct caloric energy or macronutrients, human life cannot be sustained for more than a few days without an adequate supply of fresh water.
• Water acts as the universal biological solvent in which all metabolic chemical reactions of the body take place, facilitating digestion, nutrient absorption, and cellular transport.
• Blood, lymph, and digestive juices are primarily composed of water, allowing them to flow smoothly through vessels and ducts to distribute nutrients and hormones.
• Water plays a central role in human temperature regulation through the process of sweating, where heat is dissipated from the skin surface as perspiration evaporates.
• The human body continuously loses water through urine, sweat, respiration, and bowel movements, making daily replenishment through drinking fluids and food mandatory.
• Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, leading to symptoms such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, dizziness, dark urine, and lethargy.
• Beyond drinking plain water, humans obtain significant hydration from juicy fruits like watermelons, cucumbers, oranges, soups, milk, and freshly prepared herbal teas.
• Roughage, also known as dietary fiber, consists of the indigestible plant cell wall material found in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, beans, and seeds.
• Even though roughage provides zero nutritional calories and passes through the human digestive system completely unabsorbed, it is critically important for gastrointestinal health.
• Roughage adds bulk to the stool, stimulating regular muscular contractions of the intestine known as peristalsis, which prevents chronic constipation and sluggish bowels.
• Soluble fiber helps bind to cholesterol and regulates blood sugar levels, while insoluble fiber acts like a natural brush sweeping the intestinal tract clean.
• The DAV Class 4 Science syllabus highlights that peeling fruits and vegetables often removes valuable roughage and vitamin layers located directly beneath the skin.
• Maintaining a high intake of dietary water and roughage ensures that the digestive pipeline operates efficiently, preventing toxin accumulation within the lower gut.
• Students are encouraged by DAV academic standards to carry a clean water bottle to school and develop the healthy habit of drinking sufficient water throughout the day.

• A balanced diet is scientifically defined as a daily meal plan that contains all essential nutrients—carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water, and roughage—in correct proportions.
• The exact composition of a balanced diet varies depending on an individual's age, gender, body weight, daily physical activity level, and overall health status.
• Growing children require more protein and energy-giving foods relative to their body size compared to sedentary adults, whose primary dietary focus is maintenance and repair.
• A manual laborer or professional athlete requires a much higher caloric intake, particularly from carbohydrates and fats, than an office worker who sits at a desk all day.
• Failing to consume a balanced diet results in malnutrition, which can manifest either as undernutrition (deficiency diseases) or overnutrition (obesity and lifestyle disorders).
• Deficiency diseases occur when the body lacks one or more essential nutrients over an extended period, leading to specific, recognizable clinical symptoms and organ dysfunctions.
• For instance, a lack of Vitamin A causes night blindness, a lack of Vitamin C causes scurvy, and a lack of iron causes anemia, all preventable through proper diet.
• Conversely, consuming excessive amounts of junk food, sweets, and fried items rich in empty calories leads to obesity, putting immense strain on the heart and joints.
• The DAV curriculum emphasizes that no single food item is a complete meal on its own; therefore, variety and combination are the golden rules of healthy eating.
• A traditional Indian thali, thoughtfully prepared with roti or rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, curd, and salad, serves as an excellent model of a naturally balanced meal.
• Food hygiene is an inseparable aspect of nutrition, as consuming contaminated food or water can cause severe water-borne diseases like diarrhea, typhoid, and cholera.
• Proper food preservation methods, such as refrigeration, drying, pickling, and canning, prevent the growth of harmful microorganisms and food spoilage.
• Washing fruits and vegetables thoroughly with clean water before consumption removes harmful pesticide residues, dirt, dust, and microscopic parasite eggs.
• Cooking food properly not only enhances its taste, texture, and aroma, but also kills harmful bacteria and parasites, making it safe and easy to digest.
• The DAV academic framework encourages students to avoid wasting food, reminding young learners that millions of people worldwide lack access to basic daily nutrition.

• Animals, unlike green plants, cannot manufacture their own food through photosynthesis and must rely entirely on consuming other living organisms for survival.
• Based on their specific dietary habits and the types of food they consume in their natural habitats, animals are broadly categorized into three primary nutritional groups.
• Herbivores are plant-eating animals that feed exclusively on leaves, grass, stems, roots, fruits, seeds, and bark to obtain their required nutrients and energy.
• Examples of herbivores taught in the DAV Class 4 curriculum include cows, goats, sheep, horses, elephants, rabbits, deer, and giraffes.
• Herbivores possess specialized physical adaptations, such as wide, flat grinding teeth (molars) to chew tough plant fibers and complex digestive systems to process cellulose.
• Carnivores are meat-eating animals that hunt, kill, and feed upon the flesh of other animals, obtaining high-protein and high-fat nutrition directly from prey.
• Examples of carnivorous animals include lions, tigers, leopards, wolves, sharks, eagles, snakes, and frogs, which sit higher up in the ecological food chain.
• Carnivores are equipped with sharp, pointed canine teeth and strong jaws for tearing flesh, as well as keen eyesight, hearing, or venom to capture prey.
• Omnivores are versatile animals that consume both plant matter and animal flesh as part of their regular natural diet, giving them immense ecological survival flexibility.
• Examples of omnivorous animals include humans, bears, crows, pigs, rats, domestic dogs, and hens, which can adapt to varied food availability.
• Omnivores possess a generalized set of teeth, including incisors for biting, canines for tearing, and molars for grinding both plant and animal foods.
• Scavengers and decomposers, such as vultures, hyenas, jackals, earthworms, and fungi, play a crucial environmental role by feeding on dead and decaying organic matter.
• The study of animal feeding habits illustrates the interconnectedness of nature and demonstrates how all animal life ultimately depends on primary plant producers.
• Understanding these feeding relationships forms the foundation for learning about complex ecological concepts like food chains and food webs in higher grades.
• The DAV Science curriculum highlights that every animal's body structure, from its teeth to its digestive tract, is perfectly adapted to its specific diet.

• Green plants hold a unique and fundamental position in the living world because they are the only organisms capable of making their own food using sunlight.
• The DAV curriculum introduces the remarkable biological process of photosynthesis, through which plants synthesize glucose from simple inorganic raw materials.
• The word 'photosynthesis' is derived from Greek roots: 'photo' meaning light, and 'synthesis' meaning putting together or combining elements.
• To perform photosynthesis, green plants require four essential components: sunlight, carbon dioxide gas, water, and a green pigment called chlorophyll.
• Chlorophyll is a specialized light-absorbing pigment located inside microscopic cell structures called chloroplasts, giving most plant leaves their characteristic green color.
• Plants absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil through their extensive root systems, transporting the liquid upward through specialized tissue tubes called xylem.
• Carbon dioxide gas from the surrounding air enters the plant leaves through tiny, microscopic pores called stomata, located primarily on the underside of the leaf surface.
• Sunlight energy is captured by chlorophyll molecules in the chloroplasts and is used as the driving chemical power to transform water and carbon dioxide.
• During this light-driven chemical reaction, plants convert water and carbon dioxide into glucose (sugar), which serves as their primary source of nourishment and growth.
• As a byproduct of photosynthesis, plants release pure oxygen gas into the atmosphere through the stomata, sustaining aerobic life for animals and humans.
• The chemical word equation for photosynthesis is summarized as: Carbon Dioxide + Water in the presence of Sunlight and Chlorophyll yields Glucose + Oxygen.
• Plants store their surplus manufactured food in the form of starch in various plant parts, including roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds.
• Humans and animals directly or indirectly consume these stored plant parts, making plants the ultimate universal food factory and foundation of all earthly life.
• Without the DAV-highlighted process of photosynthesis, atmospheric oxygen levels would rapidly deplete, and all heterotrophic life forms would face immediate starvation.
• Studying plant nutrition teaches students to appreciate the silent, self-sustaining nature of flora and reinforces the critical need for global environmental conservation.

• The DAV Chapter 7 study notes conclude with a comprehensive review of the fundamental themes governing food, nutrition, diet balance, and ecological dependencies.
• Food is recognized not merely as a biological necessity, but as a precious resource that connects agriculture, human health, animal behavior, and plant biology.
• The five major nutrient groups—carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals—must be harmoniously integrated into daily meals to ensure optimal physiological function.
• Water and roughage, though non-nutritive in terms of direct energy, are validated as indispensable regulators and clean-up agents of the human digestive tract.
• The DAV academic framework reinforces the vital distinction between energy-giving foods, body-building foods, and protective foods, streamlining nutritional classification.
• Understanding the dietary habits of herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores reveals the brilliant biological adaptation of animals to their respective ecological niches.
• The miraculous process of photosynthesis underscores the absolute dependence of all animal and human life on the green plant kingdom for food and oxygen.
• Maintaining food hygiene, washing produce thoroughly, cooking food correctly, and practicing proper food preservation are emphasized as vital daily health habits.
• Students are reminded that malnutrition, whether through deficiency diseases or modern obesity epidemics, can be prevented through nutritional education and balanced choices.
• The DAV Dictionary academic standard encourages young learners to apply these scientific principles to their everyday lives by making wise dietary selections.
• Respecting food, minimizing kitchen waste, and sharing meals with those in need are valuable moral lessons intertwined with the biological study of nutrition.
• The journey through Chapter 7 equips Class 4 students with a thorough, scientifically accurate understanding of how energy flows through the living world.
• Teachers utilizing these exhaustive DAV study notes can ensure complete curriculum coverage, fostering deep conceptual clarity and scientific inquiry in young minds.
• The mastery of this chapter serves as a solid intellectual springboard for exploring more intricate biological systems, food safety, and environmental science in higher classes.
• By internalizing these comprehensive DAV study notes, students are fully prepared to excel in their academic assessments and embrace a healthy, mindful lifestyle.
